primitives.name: Velocity Loss Threshold
primitives.verbatim_quote: Twenty-eight athletes were randomly assigned to a 10% velocity-loss group (VL10) or a 30% velocity-loss group (VL30).Both groups completed 8 weeks of supervised squat training twice weekly, performing four sets at 70% of one-repetition maximum, with each set terminated when the assigned threshold was reached.
primitives.assumptions: Randomized assignment, supervised training, fixed load (70% 1RM), binary threshold classification.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Thresholds below 10% or above 30% may not yield measurable performance divergence.

layer2.mapping: VL10 and VL30 map to distinct load–velocity profiles in squat training, inducing divergent physiological adaptations.

reasoning_traces.think:
The study isolates two velocity loss thresholds—10% and 30%—to evaluate their differential impact on strength and explosive performance. The 10% threshold (VL10) promotes higher mean propulsive velocity and greater explosive performance (SLJ, T30), indicating that maintaining velocity supports power development. Conversely, the 30% threshold (VL30) allows for more repetitions, enhancing strength (1RM), suggesting that fatigue-induced volume increases favor hypertrophy and maximal strength. These findings reflect a dualism in training adaptation: velocity preservation favors power, while fatigue tolerance favors strength. The statistical significance of group × time interactions underscores that these adaptations are not uniform across all outcomes. The underlying mechanism involves load–velocity–volume trade-offs, where the threshold determines the balance between mechanical stress and metabolic demand. The derived kernels suggest that strength adaptations are driven by cumulative volume under fatigue, whereas explosive performance relies on velocity maintenance. This duality implies that training prescriptions must be tailored to performance goals, with velocity loss serving as a proxy for physiological adaptation specificity.
